note: Word-by-word analysis of the dhyāna verses. Meanings are grounded in Monier-Williams (1899); the prose is written for this site.

words.translation: Her body is the deep orange-red of sindūra powder.

morphology.note: A prior member inside a longer compound, so it carries no ending of its own. The case is supplied at the far end of the word, by vigrahāṃ.

compound.gloss: as red as vermilion

children.gloss: red lead, minium, vermilion — the bright orange-red mineral powder
reddish-brown, tawny, ruddy; Monier-Williams adds that it is the colour of morning as against the darkness of night

words.note: The first member names the standard of comparison rather than a further quality, which is what makes this a karmadhāraya of the comparative kind: not "vermilion and red" but "red in the way vermilion is red". Sandhi joins the two at a + a → ā. Nothing in the word is decorative: red is the colour this whole set of verses keeps returning to.

words.translation: …and it is her body, her whole visible form, that has that colour.

morphology.note: vigraha is masculine standing alone. At the end of a bahuvrīhi describing the goddess it takes the feminine -ā and declines like any ā-stem, giving the accusative vigrahām.

compound.gloss: she whose body is vermilion-red

children.gloss: as red as vermilion
red lead, vermilion
reddish, ruddy, the colour of daybreak
individual form or shape, figure, the body

words.note: This is the word that carries the case for the whole compound, and the case is accusative — the first of a long chain of them that will not be discharged until dhyāyet arrives at the end of the fourth line. Monier-Williams gives vigraha a wide spread of senses: separation, analysis of a compound, even war; the sense wanted here is the eighth, "separate i.e. individual form or shape, the body", a form marked off from everything around it.

words.translation: She has three eyes — the right the sun, the left the moon, and between them the third, which is the twilight.

compound.gloss: she who has three eyes

children.gloss: three
the eye — literally "the leading organ", from √nī, to lead

words.note: A complete word, unlike its neighbours, and a good place to hear the difference the script insists on. sindūrāruṇa just before it has a retroflex ṇ, made with the tongue-tip curled back; trinayanā has three dental n sounds, made with the tongue-tip at the upper teeth. Nothing separates them but a syllable or two. On the three eyes the site follows Saundaryalaharī 48, quoted on this page: they are not borrowed from Śiva as an ornament but a statement about time, her looking being what divides day from night.

words.translation: A crown of rubies sits on the top of her head.

morphology.note: A prior member inside a much longer compound, so it stands in the bare stem with no ending.

compound.gloss: a crown made of rubies

children.gloss: a ruby
the head, the top of anything; a diadem, crown, crest

words.note: Monier-Williams gives mauli both "the head, the top of anything" and "a diadem, crown", and the ambiguity is useful here: mauli is also the hair piled on top of the head, which is where the moon of the next few syllables is going to sit. The whole compound this belongs to is diagrammed under śekharāṃ, where its ending finally appears.

words.translation: Something is catching the light up there — the crown, or the moon above it.

morphology.rootMeaning: to throb, quiver, twitch; to flash, glitter, sparkle
morphology.note: Present active participle in the bare stem -at, used as a compound member and so uninflected.

words.note: Two readings circulate and the compound does not decide between them: the moon flashing above the ruby crown, or the ruby crown itself flashing beneath the moon. Either way the same root is at work — √sphur is a physical word, used of a nerve twitching in the arm as readily as of light on a jewel, so the flashing here is intermittent rather than steady. In pronunciation, sph is s followed by an aspirated p, not an English f: let the breath be heard after the p. The final t assimilates to the following t of tārā, giving -sphurattārā-.

words.translation: Of the stars…

morphology.note: A prior member inside a compound: the stem keeps its long ā and takes no ending.

words.note: Monier-Williams gives tārā "a fixed star" first and "the pupil of the eye" second. Here it is a star, and it is about to be made subordinate: with the next word it forms tārānāyaka, lord of the stars, which is one of the standard ways of naming the moon without naming it. Tārā is of course also a goddess in her own right in the tantric traditions, but nothing in this compound points that way.

words.translation: …the lord: that is, the moon.

morphology.note: A prior member inside a compound, so it stands in the bare stem.

compound.gloss: lord of the stars — the moon

children.gloss: a star
a guide, leader, chief, lord

words.note: nāyaka is from √nī, "to lead", by the same derivation that gives naya, "conduct, policy" — the leader is the one who takes you somewhere. Kāvya prefers a periphrasis like this to the plain candra: calling the moon lord of the stars keeps the whole night sky in the picture at once.

words.translation: The moon flashing above her ruby diadem is the ornament worn on the crown of her head.

morphology.note: śekhara is masculine alone; at the end of a bahuvrīhi describing the goddess it becomes feminine śekharā, accusative śekharām.

compound.gloss: she whose crest-ornament is the moon, flashing above her ruby diadem
compound.vigraha: māṇikyamaulau sphuran tārānāyakaḥ śekharo yasyāḥ sā

children.gloss: a crown made of rubies
a ruby
the top of the head; a diadem, crown
the flashing lord of the stars — the moon
flashing, glittering
lord of the stars — the moon
a star
leader, lord
the crown of the head; a chaplet, diadem, crest

words.note: Five printed tokens, one word. The ending arrives only here, and it is accusative again, still waiting on dhyāyet. Note the ś of śekharāṃ: a palatal sibilant, made further back than the s of saumyāṃ and further forward than the ṣ inside vakṣoruhām — all three sibilants occur within a few words of each other in this verse.

words.translation: A smile on her face; her breasts full.

morphology.note: Two separate accusatives are printed as a single token here. āpīnavakṣoruhām, the second of them, is likewise feminine accusative singular, an ā-stem.

compound.gloss: Not one compound but two words run together by sandhi: smitamukhīm + āpīnavakṣoruhām

children.gloss: she whose face is smiling
smiled, smiling; as a noun, a smile or gentle laugh
the mouth, face, countenance
she whose breasts are full
swollen, full, round — the same family as pīna, "swelling, full, fleshy"
"that which grows on the chest" — the breast
the breast, bosom, chest
growing, sprouting on — from √ruh, and never used alone

words.note: Two sandhi joins worth slowing over. Between the words, final -īm meets initial ā- and the m simply carries across: smitamukhīm āpīna- is written smitamukhīmāpīna-. Inside the second word, vakṣas + ruha becomes vakṣoruha, because a final -as before a voiced sound turns into -o. mukha, neuter on its own, ends this bahuvrīhi as feminine mukhī, which is why the first word has an ī-stem ending and the second an ā-stem one.

words.gloss: in her two hands, a jewelled goblet filled to the brim
words.translation: She holds in her two hands a goblet of gems, full.

morphology.note: The token holds two words. pāṇibhyām is instrumental dual — a form Sanskrit keeps for things that naturally come in twos, and one of the few duals in the whole dhyāna. The second word, alipūrṇaratnacaṣakam, is accusative singular neuter: the object of bibhratīm at the end of the line.

compound.gloss: Not one compound but two words run together by sandhi: pāṇibhyām + alipūrṇaratnacaṣakam

children.gloss: with her two hands (instrumental dual of pāṇi, the hand)
a jewelled goblet, and it is full
filled with ali
a large black bee; also, in Monier-Williams, spirituous liquor
filled, full — the past participle of √pṝ, to fill
a goblet made of gems
a jewel, gem, treasure; earlier, simply a gift or wealth
a cup, wineglass, goblet

words.note: What the cup is full of is the one genuinely unsettled point in these verses. Monier-Williams gives ali two relevant senses, "a large black bee" and "spirituous liquor", and reciters split accordingly: a gem cup brimming with mead, or a gem cup with bees hovering over its sweetness. The dictionary is no help in deciding, since it also lists "spirituous liquor" under caṣaka itself. This site's commentary keeps to what the verse guarantees — a jewelled goblet — and leaves the contents where the poet left them. Note too that the number is right for a two-armed form: two hands, one cup, one lotus, and no weapon anywhere in this verse.

words.translation: And in the other hand, a red water-lily.

morphology.note: Accusative because it is a second object of bibhratīm, not because of dhyāyet.

compound.gloss: a water-lily, and a red one

children.gloss: coloured, dyed; reddened, red
the blossom of the blue lotus, Nymphaea caerulea; any water-lily

words.note: Sandhi hides the seam: rakta + utpala gives raktotpala, a + u contracting to o. Since utpala is properly the blue night-lily, specifying a red one is a deliberate move rather than a filler epithet. And rakta is worth a second look — it is the past participle of √rañj, "to be dyed, to redden", the same root that gives rāga, so the word means "reddened" and "impassioned" at once. Monier-Williams lists both senses under the one headword.

words.translation: …holding them: the cup in one hand, the lotus in the other.

morphology.rootMeaning: to bear, carry, hold; to wear; to support, maintain
morphology.note: Present active participle of a reduplicating (class 3) verb: bibharti, "she bears" → stem bibhrat-, feminine bibhratī, accusative bibhratīm.

words.note: This participle is doing two jobs at once. It agrees with the goddess, so it takes the same feminine accusative ending as every epithet around it; and being a participle it also governs objects of its own, which is why the goblet and the lotus are in the accusative independently of dhyāyet. √bhṛ is the root behind bharaṇa and bhartṛ, and its range runs from carrying an object to maintaining a household — she is not just holding these things, she is sustaining them.

words.translation: Her whole aspect is mild.
words.note: The gentleness here is literally lunar. saumya is a vṛddhi derivative of soma, and Monier-Williams puts the senses in their historical order: first "relating to Soma — the juice, the sacrifice, the moon", then "cool and moist, as opposed to hot and dry", and only then "resembling the moon: placid, gentle, mild". Set against the fierce forms of the goddess, this word is doing real work: of the four dhyāna verses, this is the only one that puts no weapon in her hands.

words.translation: Made of gems…

morphology.note: A prior member inside a compound, so it takes no ending.

words.note: Monier-Williams derives ratna from √rā, "to give", and lists "a gift, present, goods, wealth" before "a jewel, gem, treasure" — the gem is first of all something bestowed. The full compound this opens is diagrammed under raktacaraṇāṃ, three tokens along.

words.translation: …a vessel, and her feet are set on it.

morphology.note: A prior member inside a compound, so it takes no ending of its own.

compound.gloss: standing on a pot

children.gloss: a jar, pitcher, large earthen water-jar
standing, staying, situated in — from √sthā

words.note: This is the clearest upapada compound in the set. Monier-Williams marks stha "only ifc.", meaning it never appears as a word in its own right: it is a verbal root pressed flat into a compound-final, and it needs something in front of it to exist at all. The same element will return in the third verse, in padmāsanasthāṃ.

words.translation: Her reddened feet rest on a vessel of gems.

morphology.note: The feet are two, but a bahuvrīhi is resolved as a whole and agrees with the person it describes — hence feminine accusative singular, matching her and not them.

compound.gloss: she whose reddened feet rest on a jewelled vessel

children.gloss: standing on a jewelled pot
a pot made of gems
a jewel, gem
a jar, pitcher, water-pot
standing on, resting on
reddened, red
the foot

words.note: caraṇa is from √car, "to move, walk, roam": the foot named as the thing that goes. The redness is the lac dye women painted on the soles and toes, so this is an observed detail rather than a symbol, and it completes the colour scheme the verse opened with at sindūrāruṇa.

words.translation: One should meditate on her — and only now, at the end of nineteen syllables of description, does the sentence say what to do with it all.

morphology.rootMeaning: to think of, imagine, contemplate, meditate on, call to mind
morphology.note: Class-4 present stem dhyāya-, plus the optative marker -ī- and the third-singular active ending -t: dhyāya + ī + t → dhyāyet.

words.note: This is the word that makes the dhyāna a dhyāna. The optative — the tradition calls this use of it the vidhi-liṅ, the "injunctive optative" — turns what would otherwise be a portrait into an instruction: not "she is like this" but "this is how one should hold her in mind". Every accusative from sindūrāruṇa onwards has been waiting for it, which is why the verse cannot be broken into shorter sentences without losing its grammar.

words.translation: …the supreme Mother.

morphology.note: Two words are printed as one: parām, accusative singular feminine of para, and ambikām. Both are accusative because both are governed by dhyāyet — the adjective simply agrees with its noun.

compound.gloss: Not a compound — an adjective and its noun run together by sandhi: parām + ambikām

children.gloss: supreme, highest, beyond (feminine accusative singular)
the Mother (feminine accusative singular)

words.note: para begins as a word about distance — Monier-Williams opens with "far, distant, remote, on the farther side of" — and only from there becomes "supreme". What is supreme is what lies beyond. ambikā is a plain domestic word, "mother, good woman", used as a respectful form of address long before it became a name of the goddess. Putting the two together is the whole point of the verse: what is furthest beyond is addressed as the nearest thing there is. Readers inside this tradition will also hear parā, the highest of the four levels of speech, though the syntax here asks for nothing more than "supreme".

words.translation: She is red — the colour the sky takes just before the sun comes up.

morphology.note: First of a run of accusatives that will not find their verb until vibhāvaye, two lines below.

words.note: Monier-Williams glosses aruṇa "reddish-brown, tawny, red, ruddy" and then specifies it: "the colour of the morning opposed to the darkness of night". Aruṇa is also the sun's charioteer, dawn personified, so the word names a moment as much as a hue — the light before the light. The ṇ is retroflex, pulled back by the r just before it; the same happens in karuṇā and caraṇa, and it does not happen in bhavānī or vadana.

words.translation: Compassion moves across her eyes the way waves move across water.

morphology.note: akṣi, "eye", is neuter standing alone. At the end of a bahuvrīhi describing a woman it becomes -ākṣī and declines like nadī, giving the accusative -ākṣīm.

compound.gloss: she whose eyes are set rippling by compassion

children.gloss: made to move in waves by compassion
pity, compassion — one of the four brahmavihāras
wavy, waving, moving restlessly to and fro
the eye

words.note: The metaphor is built into the morphology rather than laid on top of it. taraṅga is a wave, and Monier-Williams unpacks it charmingly as taram-ga, the "across-goer", from √tṝ, to cross over. From that noun Sanskrit makes a denominative verb, taraṅgayati, "to cause to move to and fro", and taraṅgita is its past participle. So her eyes have literally been wave-d — compassion is the thing doing it, which is why karuṇā stands in an instrumental relation inside the compound. Two joins to hear: karuṇā absorbs the following a, and taraṅgita + akṣī contracts a + a to ā.

words.gloss: holding noose, goad, flower-arrow and bow
words.translation: Four hands, and in them the noose, the goad, the arrow made of flowers, and the bow.

compound.gloss: she by whom noose, goad, flower-arrow and bow are held

children.gloss: held, borne, carried — past participle of √dhṛ
noose, goad, flower-arrow and bow
children.vigraha: pāśaś cāṅkuśaś ca puṣpabāṇaś ca cāpaś ca

children.gloss: a snare, noose, tie, bond, fetter
a hook, especially an elephant-driver's hook
an arrow that is a flower
a flower, blossom
a reed-shaft, an arrow
a bow

words.note: A dvandva of four items with a participle in front of it, the whole then turned outward onto her: she is not the holding, she is the one who holds. Sandhi welds pāśa to aṅkuśa at a + a → ā, which is why the noose and the goad look like a single item in the printed line. puṣpabāṇa is the compound type the poets like best, where the first member does not qualify the second but simply is it — the arrow does not have flowers, the arrow is a flower. What the four objects mean is not this verse's business; the stotra's own next two verses take that up, and the site's cross-reference to Saundaryalaharī 7 shows the same four in the same four hands.

words.gloss: surrounded by the powers beginning with aṇimā
words.translation: The eight attainments stand around her in a ring.

morphology.rootMeaning: to cover, screen, conceal, surround, enclose
morphology.note: Past passive participle of ā + √vṛ. The token also carries a second word in front of it, aṇimādibhiḥ, instrumental plural — "by those beginning with aṇimā".

compound.gloss: Not a compound — two words joined by sandhi: aṇimādibhiḥ + āvṛtām

children.gloss: the set that has aṇimā for its first member — aṇimā and the rest
minuteness, fineness; the power of becoming as small as an atom
beginning; at the end of a compound, "beginning with, and so on"
surrounded, encompassed (feminine accusative singular)

words.note: The eight siddhis that this phrase gestures at are aṇimā, laghimā, mahimā, prāpti, prākāmya, īśitva, vaśitva and kāmāvasāyitā — the powers to become minute, to become weightless, to become vast, to reach anywhere, to have one's will unobstructed, to command, to subdue, and to have every wish already fulfilled. The compound names only the first and lets ādi carry the rest, which is standard Sanskrit shorthand. Two points of form: aṇiman is an -an stem and drops its final n before a compound member, exactly as rājan gives rāja-; and at the word join, final -bhiḥ becomes -bhir before the vowel of āvṛtām.

words.translation: They ring her like rays thrown off her own body; and I contemplate her as nothing other than "I".

morphology.note: Four words are printed as one token. mayūkhaiḥ is instrumental plural and belongs with āvṛtām in the phrase before it. aham is the nominative singular pronoun "I", quoted rather than construed. iti closes the quotation, and eva narrows it.

compound.gloss: Not a compound — four words joined by sandhi: mayūkhaiḥ + aham + iti + eva

children.gloss: with rays, as rays (instrumental plural of mayūkha, a ray of light)
I (nominative singular)
thus, so — the particle that closes a quotation and points back at it
just, only, exactly, nothing but

words.note: The most consequential four syllables in the dhyāna are hiding inside a token that looks like one long word. aham ity eva is a quotation: the thing contemplated is the word "I". eva is the restrictive particle — Monier-Williams says its main job is to strengthen whatever it follows — so the sense is not "I contemplate her, and also myself" but "I contemplate her as just this and nothing else: I". mayūkha itself is a homely word before it is a radiant one; the dictionary's first sense is a wooden peg for hanging cloth on, then the gnomon of a sundial, and only then a ray of light. Sandhi runs the whole chain together: -aiḥ becomes -air before a vowel, and iti + eva contracts to ity eva.

words.translation: I make her present to myself by imagining her.

morphology.rootMeaning: to be, become — with the prefix vi- and the causative -aya-, to cause to appear, to make manifest, to bring clearly before the mind
morphology.note: Causative stem bhāvaya-, "cause to be", with the prefix vi-, in the ātmanepada first singular: vibhāvaya + e → vibhāvaye. The middle ending marks the action as done by the speaker for the speaker.

words.note: Everything turns on the causative. Monier-Williams glosses the related vibhāvana as "causing to appear, developing, manifesting", and vibhāvita as "caused to arise or appear" — so this is not "I see her" or "I worship her" but something closer to "I bring her into appearance". Compare dhyāyet in the first and third verses: there someone is told what should be done, in the third person and at a distance. Here the speaker steps forward and says what he is doing, in the first person and in the middle voice, which in Sanskrit is precisely the voice for an action that comes back on the doer.

words.translation: …Bhavānī.

morphology.note: Formed from bhava with the feminine suffix -ānī, the same suffix behind indrāṇī, rudrāṇī and śarvāṇī. It declines like nadī: accusative singular bhavānīm.

words.note: The object the whole verse has been reaching for. Bhava is one of the oldest names of Śiva, so Bhavānī is "she who belongs to Bhava" — but bhava is also an ordinary noun, and Monier-Williams lists its senses first: "coming into existence, birth, production", then "being, existence, life", then "worldly existence, the world". Both readings are live in a text like this one. She is Śiva's, and she is what coming-into-being belongs to.

words.translation: One should meditate on her — and this time the instruction comes first, so everything after it is already known to be a thing to hold in mind.

morphology.rootMeaning: to think of, imagine, contemplate, meditate on, call to mind
morphology.note: Class-4 present stem dhyāya-, the optative marker -ī-, and the third-singular active ending -t: dhyāya + ī + t → dhyāyet.

words.note: The same verb that ended the first verse now opens the third, and the difference in placement changes how the verse is read aloud. In the first, nineteen syllables of description have to be carried in suspense before the verb resolves them; here the verb lands at once and the twelve epithets that follow can be taken one at a time. Both are optatives, and in both the force is the same: this is what one should do, not what happens to be the case.

words.translation: Her seat is a lotus, and she is sitting in it in the lotus posture.

morphology.note: Accusative, governed by the dhyāyet that has just been spoken.

compound.gloss: seated on a lotus throne

children.gloss: a seat that is a lotus
a lotus, especially the flower of Nelumbium speciosum, which closes towards evening
sitting, a sitting posture; a seat, place, stool
standing on, seated in — from √sthā, and never used alone

words.note: The word says two things at once and the dictionary confirms both. āsana means a seat, and it also means a yogic posture — Monier-Williams's second sense for it is "sitting in a peculiar posture according to the custom of devotees", and the very first example he names is padmāsana. So padmāsanasthā is both "she who is on a lotus seat" and "she who is in the lotus posture". The second dhyāna verse never said where she was sitting; this one does, and the site's cross-reference to Saundaryalaharī 8 supplies the rest of the setting.

words.translation: Her face has opened the way a flower opens.

compound.gloss: she whose face is open and bright

children.gloss: opened, expanded, budded, blown — the past participle of vi + √kas
the mouth, face, countenance — literally the speaking part, from √vad

words.note: vikasita is the ordinary word for a flower coming open, and Monier-Williams gives the verb vi-√kas both "to open, expand, blossom" and "to shine, be bright, beam with joy". Applied to a face seated on a lotus, it keeps the two senses in contact: her expression does what the flower under her is doing. English has to choose between "blossoming" and "beaming"; Sanskrit does not.

words.translation: Her eyes are drawn out long, the shape of a lotus petal.

morphology.note: As in karuṇātaraṅgitākṣīṃ, the neuter akṣi becomes -ākṣī at the end of a bahuvrīhi describing a woman, and declines like nadī.

compound.gloss: she whose eyes are as long as the petal of a lotus
compound.vigraha: padmapatre iva āyate akṣiṇī yasyāḥ sā

children.gloss: long in the way a lotus petal is long
the petal of a lotus
a lotus
a leaf, a petal
stretched, extended, drawn out long — the past participle of ā + √yam
the eye

words.note: Monier-Williams files the word for leaf under pattra and notes that patra is a later spelling; his gloss is worth having in mind here, because he defines the petal as "regarded as the plumage of a tree or flower", the first senses of the word being wing, pinion and feather. The comparison in this compound is therefore not only about shape. āyata, from ā + √yam, "to stretch out", is what a bowstring does — the eye is drawn, not merely long. Sandhi joins āyata to akṣī at a + a → ā.

words.translation: The light coming off her is the colour of gold.

compound.gloss: she whose sheen is that of gold

children.gloss: gold — the compound form of heman
splendour, light, a flash; colour, appearance; a reflected image

words.note: Here the four dhyāna verses openly part company. The first made her the colour of vermilion, the fourth will make her the colour of hibiscus, and this one makes her gold. The site's commentary takes the disagreement at face value: these verses come from different places and were never meant to be one picture. ābhā is a nicely unstable word — Monier-Williams runs it from "splendour, light" through "colour, appearance" to "a reflected image, likeness, resemblance", so what is gold may be her body or only the light she throws. Sandhi: hema + ābhā, a + ā → ā.

words.translation: Her garment is yellow.

compound.gloss: she whose cloth is yellow

children.gloss: yellow — the colour Monier-Williams assigns to the Vaiśyas, as white is to Brāhmans and red to Kṣatriyas
cloth, clothes, garment, dress

words.note: A useful reminder that Sanskrit dictionaries number their homonyms for a reason. Monier-Williams's first pīta is the past participle of √pā, "drunk, sipped, quaffed"; the pīta that means "yellow" is a separate word listed further down the same entry, possibly from √pyai and named, he suggests, after the colour of butter and oil. The forms are identical, and only the sense of the compound tells you which one is in front of you.

words.gloss: a shining golden lotus held in her hand
words.translation: A lotus of gold, catching the light, rests in her hand.

compound.gloss: she in whose hand a glittering golden lotus is held
compound.vigraha: kare kalitaṃ lasad dhemapadmaṃ yasyāḥ sā

children.gloss: held in the hand
the hand — literally "the doer", from √kṛ
held, borne, taken up; furnished or provided with
a lotus of gold, and it is glittering
shining, glittering, playing — present participle of √las
a lotus made of gold
gold
a lotus

words.note: This is the one place in the dhyāna where a conjunct consonant hides a word boundary. lasat ends in t and hema begins with h; the t voices to d and the h is pulled along with it into dh, so the two become lasaddhema and the seam disappears from the page. Reading the compound is largely a matter of finding that seam again. √las is a pleasant root to know: Monier-Williams gives it "to shine, flash, glitter", but also "to play, sport, frolic" and "to dance", and lāsya, the graceful dance, comes from it. The lotus is not merely bright; it is playing with the light.

words.translation: Every part of her is well made.

morphology.note: aṅga is neuter alone; ending a bahuvrīhi applied to a woman it takes the feminine -ī, giving varāṅgī, accusative varāṅgīm.

compound.gloss: she whose limbs are the choicest

children.gloss: choicest, valuable, precious, best, most excellent
a limb, member; the body; a subordinate part of anything

words.note: vara is from √vṛ, "to choose": the best is what would be chosen. Monier-Williams records varāṅga both as a neuter noun, "the best member of the body", meaning the head, and as an adjective, "having an excellent form, excellent or beautiful in all parts" — the adjectival sense is the one at work here, since the word has to agree with her. Sandhi joins the two members at a + a → ā.

words.translation: She is decked in ornaments of every kind.

compound.gloss: joined with all the ornaments

children.gloss: all the ornaments there are
whole, entire, all, every
the act of decorating; an ornament, decoration
yoked, joined, furnished with — past participle of √yuj

words.note: alaṅkāra is alam, "enough, sufficiently", plus √kṛ, "to make": an ornament is what brings a thing up to the mark. The same word is the technical term for a figure of speech, which is why Sanskrit poetics is called alaṅkāraśāstra — poems are adorned the way bodies are. Monier-Williams files the headword as alaṃkāra; this text writes the nasal as ṅ before the k, which is the same sound spelled to match its neighbour. yukta is from √yuj, so the ornaments are yoked to her rather than merely placed on her.

words.translation: Constantly — not now and then.

morphology.note: An adverb, the neuter accusative of satata pressed into adverbial service. It takes no further ending and never changes shape.

words.note: The printed line breaks in the wrong place. What the poet wrote is satatam abhayadām, two words; this recension sets the break after satata and hands the final m to the following token, so both halves are fragments. Monier-Williams derives satata from saṃ-tata, "stretched together, continuous", with the nasal lost exactly as in sa-hita for saṃ-hita — tata being the past participle of √tan, to stretch. So "constantly" is literally "in one unbroken stretch", which is the point of the epithet it governs.

words.translation: She gives fearlessness, and gives it without interruption.

morphology.note: The m that opens this token is not part of the word: it is the last letter of satatam, carried across by the printed line break. The word itself is abhayadām.

compound.gloss: she who gives freedom from fear

children.gloss: absence of fear, safety, security — the negative prefix a- on bhaya, fear
giving, granting — the bare root √dā, which Monier-Williams marks as occurring only at the end of a compound

words.note: An upapada compound of the same kind as ghaṭastha in the first verse: -dā cannot stand on its own and exists only as the tail of a word. The epithet is the verbal twin of the abhaya-mudrā, the open palm raised in the gesture of reassurance that this goddess is almost always shown making, though the verse names the act and not the gesture. Read with satatam in front of it, the claim is about duration: the granting does not lapse.

words.translation: She bends toward those who have given themselves to her.

compound.gloss: bending toward her devotees

children.gloss: devoted, attached; a devotee — past participle of √bhaj, to share, apportion, be devoted to
bowing, inclining, bent; submissive, humble; bowing to (at the end of a compound)

words.note: This is the one epithet in the dhyāna whose direction is genuinely disputed. namra is active in form and sense — Monier-Williams gives "bowing, inclining" and, for the compounded use, "bowing to" — which makes the natural reading the one taken here: she is the one who inclines, and her devotees are what she inclines toward. Many reciters render it the other way, "she to whom devotees bow", which reads namra as though it were passive. The grammar favours the first; the devotional habit favours the second; the compound itself does not say, and a reader is entitled to hold both.

words.translation: Bhavānī — the name the second verse ended on, here in the middle of the chain rather than at its close.

morphology.note: bhava plus the feminine suffix -ānī, declined like nadī. Written here with anusvāra, bhavānīṃ, because the next word begins with ś.

words.note: The only proper name shared between two of the four verses, which is part of why the second and third are often printed together. Its position is different, though: in the second verse it is the last word and receives vibhāvaye; here it is one epithet among a dozen, and the sentence keeps going past it for another whole line.

words.translation: She is called Śrīvidyā outright — not a goddess who possesses a mantra, but the mantra itself wearing a body.

compound.gloss: the knowledge that is itself radiance and good fortune

children.gloss: light, lustre, radiance, splendour, beauty; prosperity, good fortune, majesty, royal dignity
knowledge, science, learning; also a spell, an incantation

words.note: Everything depends on which sense of vidyā is heard. Monier-Williams gives "knowledge, science, learning" first and "a spell, incantation" third, and in this tradition the third is technical: a vidyā is a goddess's mantra, and Śrīvidyā is the name both of the fifteen-syllabled mantra and of the whole system built around it. The nyāsa printed just before these verses spells that out, naming the three segments of the mantra as bīja, śakti and kīlaka — which is the tradition's way of saying that the thousand names to come are that mantra written out at length. The compound can also be read as a tatpuruṣa, "the knowledge belonging to Śrī"; the karmadhāraya taken here, in which the knowledge simply is the radiance, is the reading the tradition prefers.

words.translation: Her form is a settled, quieted one.

morphology.note: mūrti is a feminine i-stem, so the accusative singular is mūrtim — written here with anusvāra before the s of sakala-.

compound.gloss: she whose embodied form is at peace

children.gloss: appeased, pacified, tranquil, calm, free from passions — past participle of √śam
any solid body or material form; embodiment, manifestation; an image, statue

words.note: Because mūrti is already feminine, the compound can be parsed two ways with no change of ending: as the bahuvrīhi taken here, "she whose form is peaceful", or as a karmadhāraya, "peace given a body", śāntā cāsau mūrtiś ca. Both are recited. The root behind śānta is √śam, "to come to rest, be quiet, be satisfied", the root of śānti and of the śam that opens so many Vedic benedictions; and mūrti is the ordinary word for a temple image, so the epithet quietly says that what is being described is a form made for looking at.

words.translation: There is no god who does not praise her.

compound.gloss: praised by the gods, all of them

children.gloss: the entire body of gods
consisting of all its parts, complete, entire, whole
a god, divinity, deity
praised, commended — past participle of √nu, to praise

words.note: Two small etymologies that repay a look. sakala is sa + kalā, "having its parts", so "entire" is arrived at by addition rather than by asserting a whole. And sura, the ordinary word for a god, is according to Monier-Williams probably a back-formation: asura was misread as a-sura, as though it carried a negative prefix, and the positive was invented to match. The gods are named after the demons they are not.

words.translation: Every kind of…

morphology.note: A prior member inside a compound, so it takes no ending. Standing alone sarva declines as a pronoun rather than as an ordinary adjective.

words.note: Its second appearance in two lines — sarvālaṅkāra- opened line 9 — and both times it is doing the same work, refusing to let the epithet be partial. Monier-Williams notes that sarva is inflected as a pronoun and serves as the model for a whole class of pronominals. The full compound it begins here is diagrammed under the next token, where the ending finally arrives.

words.translation: …good fortune, and she is the one who gives it. The verb spoken at the very start of the verse finally has its object.

morphology.note: Agent nouns in -tṛ make their feminine in -trī and then decline like nadī: accusative singular -trīm.

compound.gloss: she who bestows prosperity of every kind

children.gloss: every kind of good fortune
whole, entire, all, every
success, accomplishment, fulfilment; acquisition, possession, advantage, blessing
a giver, bestower — the feminine agent noun of pra + √dā, to give forth

words.note: The final -d of sampad devoices to -t before the voiceless p of pradātrī, which is why the printed word reads sampat-. sampad is itself sam + √pad, "to fall together, to come out right", so prosperity in Sanskrit is a matter of things landing in the right arrangement rather than of accumulation. Monier-Williams even records sampatpradā, "bestowing fortune", as an established name of a form of Bhairavī — the epithet was already a title before this verse used it.

words.gloss: smeared with saffron, musk touching her forehead
words.translation: Saffron paste on her body, and a mark of musk that just reaches her forehead.

morphology.note: Two words are printed as one token. Both are feminine accusative singular and both describe her: sakuṅkumavilepanām, and then alikacumbikastūrikām.

compound.gloss: Not one compound but two epithets joined by sandhi: sakuṅkumavilepanām + alikacumbikastūrikām

children.gloss: she who wears an unguent of saffron
with, accompanied by — the prefix that turns the whole word into a bahuvrīhi
an ointment of saffron
saffron — Crocus sativus, both the plant and the pollen of its flowers
smearing, anointing; an unguent, ointment, perfume for the person
she whose musk-mark touches her forehead
kissing the forehead
the forehead
kissing, touching — an agent form of √cumb, to kiss, to touch with the mouth
musk, the animal perfume; also the musk-deer itself

words.note: The sa- at the head of the first word is worth marking, because this verse uses it three times: sakuṅkuma-, samanda-, saśara-. It is the cheapest way Sanskrit has of making a bahuvrīhi — prefix sa- to a noun and the whole thing becomes an adjective meaning "having that". On cumbika: Monier-Williams has the root √cumb, "to kiss, to touch with the mouth", and the agent forms cumbaka and cumbin, but not cumbika, which is the same formation with the -ka suffix; many printings give alikacumbi-kastūrikām, with cumbin instead. The sense is unaffected — the musk does not sit on the forehead so much as brush it. This is also the word the metre cuts in half: the pṛthvī pause falls after the eighth syllable, inside vilepana, so the break should be heard without opening a gap in the sound.

words.gloss: a faint smile in her glance
words.translation: Her look carries the beginning of a smile rather than a full one.

compound.gloss: she whose glance comes with a slight smile in it

children.gloss: with, accompanied by
a faint laugh, a half-smile
slow, soft, faint, slack, gentle — used of light, of a voice, of rain and wind
laughing, smiling; as a noun, laughter — past participle of √has
a look, view, glance, sight; also the eye itself

words.note: The precision is in manda. Monier-Williams's senses for it are all about something running below its full strength — slow, faint, slack, low, gentle — so mandahasita is not a smile but a laugh turned down, √has being the root for laughing outright. And the smile is placed in the īkṣaṇa, the glance, not on the mouth: what is being described is a way of looking. Sandhi hides the join, hasita + īkṣaṇa contracting a + ī to e, so the compound has to be cut at -hasit-ekṣaṇā rather than where the eye first wants to cut it.

words.gloss: bearing arrow, bow, noose and goad
words.translation: She carries the arrow, the bow, the noose and the goad.

compound.gloss: she who has arrow, bow, noose and goad about her

children.gloss: with, accompanied by
arrow, bow, noose and goad
children.vigraha: śaraś ca cāpaś ca pāśaś cāṅkuśaś ca

children.gloss: a reed of the kind arrows are made from; an arrow, shaft
a bow
a snare, noose, bond, fetter
a hook, especially an elephant-driver's hook

words.note: The same four objects as the second dhyāna verse, in a different order and reached by a different route: there a participle, dhṛta-, said they were held; here the bare prefix sa- says only that they are with her. Note also that this verse says śara where the other said puṣpabāṇa — the plain arrow rather than the arrow of flowers. Saundaryalaharī 7, quoted on this page, gives the oldest and most famous version of the same four hands.

words.translation: No creature is left out of it: every one of them is thrown off balance by her.

morphology.note: Stems in -in form their feminine in -inī and then decline like nadī: accusative singular -inīm.

compound.gloss: she who bewilders all beings

children.gloss: every creature, with none left over
without remainder, entire, all — the negative a- on śeṣa, remainder
a creature, living being, person; people collectively
deluding, confusing, perplexing, illusive — from the causative of √muh

words.note: Softer translations make this "she who enchants everyone", but Monier-Williams is blunter: mohin is "deluding, confusing, perplexing, illusive", and the root √muh means to become stupefied, to be bewildered, to go astray. What she does to beings is closer to disorientation than to charm — and Mohinī is of course also the name of the form Viṣṇu took to bewilder the demons out of the nectar. Grammatically, agent nouns in -in govern an accusative, which is what lets aśeṣajana- stand as their object inside the compound. aśeṣa is worth keeping: not "all" as a total, but "with nothing left over".

words.gloss: red garland, red ornaments, red robes
words.translation: Garland, jewellery and clothing are all the same red.

compound.gloss: she whose garland, ornaments and garments are all ruddy

children.gloss: reddish, ruddy, the colour of daybreak
garland, ornament and garment
a wreath, garland, chaplet
ornament, decoration
clothes, apparel, garment; also the sky

words.note: One adjective is made to cover three nouns at once, which is what a dvandva inside a bahuvrīhi is for. Sandhi joins bhūṣā to ambara at ā + a → ā, so the last two look like one item. ambara is a word poets enjoy, since it means both a garment and the sky and either can be draped; here the garland and the ornaments beside it settle the sense. This is the third dhyāna verse to insist on red, after the sindūra of the first and the aruṇā that opens the second — the site's commentary reads that insistence as a statement about icchā, desire understood as the first stirring by which anything comes to be.

words.translation: She is as bright as the scarlet japā blossom.

morphology.note: The last of the accusatives, and the one immediately before the verb that governs them all.

compound.gloss: radiant in the way the hibiscus blossom is radiant

children.gloss: the flower of the japā plant
the China rose, Hibiscus rosa-sinensis
a flower, blossom
shining, radiant, bright, splendid — from √bhās, to shine

words.note: Like sindūrāruṇa at the very beginning of the dhyāna, this is a karmadhāraya of comparison: the first member is not a further quality but the thing being compared to. The japā is the deep scarlet hibiscus offered to the goddess in worship, and the comparison was standard long before this verse — Monier-Williams records japākusumasaṃnibha, "resembling the japā flower", as a compound in its own right. Keep the vowel lengths clean here, because the next word is japavidhau with a short a: the flower and the recitation are two different words that the poet has deliberately set side by side.

words.translation: This is the form to hold in mind at the moment of counting the mantra.

morphology.note: Locative singular of an i-stem: vidhi → vidhau. This is the only locative in the whole dhyāna.

compound.gloss: the rite of muttered recitation

children.gloss: muttering prayers, repeating scripture or the names of a deity in a low murmuring tone
a rule, injunction, precept; any prescribed act, rite or ceremony

words.note: One word changes the standing of the entire verse. Every other word in the dhyāna is either an accusative describing her or a verb governing those accusatives; this locative names an occasion, and in doing so tells you when the verse is for. The fourth dhyāna is the only one of the four that announces its own use. Note also that japa is defined by its volume — Monier-Williams's gloss turns on the murmuring, not on the words being said — and that vidhi is the same word the ritual manuals use for a prescribed procedure, so "japavidhau" is roughly "when you get to the recitation section".

words.gloss: I call the Mother to mind
words.translation: I call the Mother to mind — and the four verses close on the same word the first of them ended with.

morphology.rootMeaning: to remember, recollect, bear in mind, call to mind, think of
morphology.note: Class-1 present stem smara- with the first-singular parasmaipada ending -mi. The token also carries the object, ambikām, feminine accusative singular.

compound.gloss: Not a compound — a verb and its object joined by sandhi: smarāmi + ambikām

children.gloss: I remember, I call to mind
the Mother (feminine accusative singular of ambikā)

words.note: The sandhi is the ordinary one for a final i meeting a following vowel: smarāmi + ambikām gives smarāmy ambikām, printed here as one word. √smṛ carries more weight than "remember" suggests in English — it is the root behind smṛti, the whole class of remembered texts, and Monier-Williams's entry runs from recollecting to handing down and reciting. Set beside the other three verbs of the dhyāna it completes a range: dhyāyet says what one should do, vibhāvaye says the speaker is causing her to appear, and smarāmi says only that he is calling to mind something already known. The set began with parām ambikām and ends with ambikām; the last word is the first word, minus the distance.
